options.text: Sending many concurrent request/response streams over a single connection

questions.explanation: HTTP/2 interleaves many streams over one connection, so requests no longer wait one-at-a-time as they did in HTTP/1.1 — which is why sharding/concatenation matter less.

questions.prompt: What problem does HTTP/3 (over QUIC) solve that HTTP/2 still has?

options.text: TCP-level head-of-line blocking, where one lost packet stalls all streams

questions.explanation: HTTP/2 rides on TCP, so a single lost packet stalls every stream on the connection. QUIC's independent streams (over UDP) prevent one loss from stalling the others, and set up connections faster.

questions.prompt: HTTP/3 runs over a UDP-based transport protocol called ____.
questions.explanation: QUIC is the transport under HTTP/3; it provides independent streams, integrated TLS 1.3 (faster setup), and connection migration.

questions.prompt: Which statements are true? Select all that apply.

options.text: HTTP/2 multiplexes many streams over one connection
Domain sharding can hurt on HTTP/2 by fragmenting multiplexing
A CDN caches content on edge servers near users to cut latency

questions.explanation: HTTP/2 multiplexes, sharding fragments that benefit, and CDNs cut latency at the edge. But HTTP/2 still has TCP-level head-of-line blocking, which HTTP/3 addresses.

questions.prompt: Match each technology to its description.

pairs.right: Runs over QUIC with independent streams
Edge caches near users that offload the origin

questions.explanation: HTTP evolved from one-at-a-time (1.1) to multiplexed (2) to QUIC-based (3); a CDN is orthogonal, cutting distance by caching at the edge.

questions.prompt: Order the HTTP protocols by version, oldest to newest.
questions.explanation: The web moved from HTTP/1.1 (serial) to HTTP/2 (multiplexed over TCP) to HTTP/3 (multiplexed over QUIC/UDP).
